Lessons.Title: Different Ways to Solve Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Represent and solve multi-step word problems using multiplication and division, interpreting products and quotients in context. Compare different valid strategies rather than insisting on one algorithm.

2021 teacher sequence: Which One Doesn't Belong? expressions worth 450; museum field trip (45 students, $18 tickets, $900 budget), multiple solution strategies; movie ticket sales ($9, $3,132 first-day revenue, equal sales the next day), refreshments; synthesis; protected publisher Cool-down.

Explain what every result measures. A museum budget requires multiplying to find total ticket cost before deciding whether sufficient money remains. Different ways to partition 45×18 lead to the same $810 cost.

To determine two-day movie attendance, first divide the first-day revenue by the price of a ticket, then double the resulting daily ticket count. Each person's two-item refreshment price is the sum of the two item prices.

Teacher-led work: compare five source strategies on classroom posters, use another strategy for 14×35, and co-craft student questions. Oral justification and independent question writing are not machine-graded as correct solely from numeric input.
First-party Edulytics Cool-down (not publisher original): 28 $17 tickets purchased from a $500 budget leave $24.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare a product with a budget
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total cost of equal-price tickets is the number of people multiplied by price.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compute price×quantity before subtracting from budget.

KeyConcepts.Title: Find a quantity from total and price
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total ticket revenue divided by ticket price counts the tickets sold.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Label daily versus two-day quantities and multiply by the number of equal-sales days.

KeyConcepts.Title: Combine multiple per-person purchases
KeyConcepts.Definition: The whole amount from multiple purchases per attendee equals attendee count multiplied by their combined price.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add drink and popcorn prices before multiplying by the two-day count.

WorkedExamples.Title: Museum trip: tickets and remaining money
WorkedExamples.Question: 45 students need museum tickets at $18 each and teachers have $900. Is the budget enough? How much is left?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply to find cost, then subtract from budget.

WorkedExamples.Title: Alternate multiplication strategy
WorkedExamples.Question: After comparing the source museum strategies, compute 14×35 in two different ways.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the distributive property with two decompositions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both partitions produce the same product.

WorkedExamples.Title: Movie tickets across two equal days
WorkedExamples.Question: Movie tickets cost $9 each; the theater earned $3,132 on day one and sold the same quantity on day two. How many tickets altogether?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide daily ticket revenue by unit price, then double.
Steps: Day two has 348 tickets as well.

WorkedExamples.Title: Popcorn and drinks for all moviegoers
WorkedExamples.Question: Each of 696 ticket holders buys a $7 drink and $5 popcorn. How much do both items bring in over both days?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add per-person prices, then multiply by attendee count.
Steps: The two items cost 7+5=12 dollars per person.
There were 696 ticket holders over the two days.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent Edulytics Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: 28 students buy $17 tickets with a $500 budget. How many dollars remain?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the budget $900 as the cost of 45 tickets.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate ticket cost first, and then subtract from the available budget.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating $3,132 as ticket revenue across both days.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source says $3,132 was collected on the first day only.
CommonMistakes.Correction: 3132÷9=348 tickets per day and 696 tickets for two days.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying attendance by just $7 or just $5.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The student-facing source explicitly says each ticket holder buys both items.

SummaryPoints: Strategies such as 20−2 per ticket, partial products, and factors give the same product.
The theater sold 3132÷9=348 tickets/day and 696 over two days.
Buying $7 and $5 items per attendee leads to $8,352 total.
Teacher evaluates source strategy posters, original diagrams and student-created questions; the Cool-down 28×17 is first-party Edulytics.
